Title (auto): A Modular Framework for Automated Evaluation of Procedural Content Generation in Serious Games With Deep Reinforcement Learning Agents
Authors/Year/Venue: Kalafatis, E., Mitsis, K., Zarkogianni, K., Athanasiou, M. and Nikita, K. (2025). IEEE Transactions on Games, vol. 17, no. 4, pp. 1003-1012. DOI 10.1109/TG.2025.3589439
Game / environment: Wake Up for the Future, an open-world serious game on obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) with card duels against NPCs. Three versions of the game that differ only in NPC generation. Game logic rewritten in GDL (pygdl) and wrapped as a Gymnasium environment
Primary goal: PCG evaluation (comparing PCG versions in a serious game through the training and win rate of DRL test agents)
Role of PCG: Generated content is the object under test. Version 1 random NPC creation (baseline), versions 2 and 3 GA-based NPC creation. The PCG makes NPC attribute profiles (3 of 7 attributes), not levels or maps
AI technique: RL (PPO from Stable-Baselines3 as the test agent). A genetic algorithm is the PCG under test and is not the testing method
Agent / persona: Goal-driven (agent is rewarded for winning card duels and for impactful moves, no persona or human-like model)
Human data?: No (the human study of the same game is cited from an earlier paper and not used here)
Tools / benchmarks: Stable-Baselines3 (PPO), Gymnasium, pygdl and Game Description Language, Unity game adapted for the framework, Metrics Logger. No public benchmark
Metrics: Agent win rate, cumulative reward, number of games played, appearance frequency of each NPC attribute, training speed. Shapiro-Wilk, Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney U tests, IQR outlier removal
Scale: 3 game versions, 20 agents (random seeds) trained on each version for 1 000 000 game actions, a comprehensive test on all 35 three-attribute NPC combinations played 5 times per agent, a scenario-based test with 60 best agent instances against 1000 random and 1000 GA-generated NPCs (outlier agents removed)
Key results (+page): Agents trained on versions 2 and 3 reach a 97 percent peak win rate vs 94 percent for version 1 and pass 50 percent win rate earlier in training. Scenario test Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.007 on random NPCs and p = 0.008 on PCG NPCs. Version 1 vs 3 p = 0.002 and 0.015, version 1 vs 2 p = 0.029 and 0.040. Versions 2 and 3 do not differ significantly (pp.1008-1010)
Stated limitations: Only one serious game, so generalisation is unknown. Only PPO used and it is not designed for game testing. Baseline is plain random generation, a structured random baseline would be fairer. No human participants or interviews. Metrics still need human interpretation (p.1011)
Future work: More showcase games from other genres and other PCG types, compare more DRL algorithms, add interviews with human players, add an automated interpreter for the metrics, add explainable AI to link agent decisions to the serious purpose (p.1011)
RQ1 Methods/tools: Modular four-space framework (serious game, interaction interpreter, DRL, testing) where PPO agents are trained on each PCG version and their win rate and training curves are compared. Built on Stable-Baselines3, Gymnasium and GDL
RQ2 Properties evaluated: Effect of the NPC generator on agent learning speed and win rate, balance of NPC attribute frequency (about 42 percent against 42.9 percent expected), and whether the PCG adapts difficulty to the agent (attribute rotation follows win rate changes)
RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: Random NPC generation (version 1) is the baseline. 20 seeds with nonparametric tests, comprehensive and scenario-based tests. No human comparison inside the study. Authors admit a structured random baseline is missing
RQ4 Limitations/open problems: Single game, single RL algorithm, simple random baseline, no human validation, manual interpretation of results, agent behaviour not yet explained
Reviewer comment: One of the clearest papers that tests the PCG itself with agents, so a strong PCG match. Content is NPC attributes and not spatial levels, so transfer to level generation is an argument and not a result. No code or data link (Q2 = 0). Abstract reports p = 0.009 but the body reports 0.007 and 0.008 so we quote the body. IEEE TG is a games venue, not an SE venue
Comparison baseline: Random (random NPC generation, version 1)
Testing budget: 1 000 000 game actions per agent and version, 20 agents x 3 versions, trained instances saved every 10 000 actions, wall-clock time NR in text (p.1008)
Testing objective: Compare PCG variants by agent win rate and training behaviour, check that generated NPC content stays balanced and adapts to the agent

Title (auto): Playtesting: What is Beyond Personas
Authors/Year/Venue: Ariyurek, S., Surer, E. and Betin-Can, A. (2023). IEEE Transactions on Games, vol. 15, no. 3, pp. 348-359. DOI 10.1109/TG.2022.3165882
Game / environment: GVGAI 2D grid game (avatar, exit, monsters, treasures, walls), a 2D Doom testbed and a 3D Doom testbed in VizDoom
Genre: Other (2D grid adventure testbed and Doom first-person shooter testbeds)
Primary goal: Player-experience modelling (developing personas with several goals) and Coverage-exploration (alternative paths that reach the same goal)
AI technique: RL (PPO, with CTS or ICM exploration and the proposed APF reward modulation)
Agent / persona: Persona-based (4 procedural personas and 5 developing personas with handcrafted utility functions)
Human data?: No (persona goals and utilities are handcrafted)
Tools / benchmarks: GVGAI framework, VizDoom, PPO from the Stable Baselines project, CTS and ICM exploration models, APF CTS and APF ICM
Metrics: Interactions with game objects, generated trajectories and total discounted reward, trajectory length
Scale: 3 testbeds, 4 procedural and 5 developing personas, stochastic games evaluated 1000 times per trained agent

RQ2 Properties evaluated: Diversity and coverage of play traces, ability of personas to change goals, and discovery of alternative paths to the same goal. No generated content evaluated
RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: Compared with fixed-goal procedural personas and with PPO agents without APF (also PPO with CTS or ICM), using small testbeds and mostly descriptive comparison without statistical tests
RQ4 Limitations/open problems: Subjective notion of a different path, reward side effects, sensitivity to noise, data needs and only small testbeds
Reviewer comment: Clear methodological paper on playtesting diversity. Useful for PCG because diverse traces could explore generated levels, but the paper does not test that, so it is a transfer argument. No code link (Q2 = 0). The paper reports no significance tests, though baselines are present. Published in vol. 15 (2023), the DOI year 2022 is the online date
Comparison baseline: Other (procedural personas, plain PPO and PPO with CTS or ICM)
Testing budget: NR (1000 evaluation runs for the stochastic games, episodes capped at 200 timesteps in GVGAI and 2000 in Doom, training time not reported)
Testing objective: Generate more diverse and informative play traces while keeping the agent's goal, and find alternative paths

Title (auto): A New Approach to Evaluating Diversity and Difficulty in Procedurally Generated 2D Platformer Game Levels Through the Relationship Between Structural Metrics and Game Mechanic Constraints in Intelligent Agents
Authors/Year/Venue: Perez, S. & Rojas, D. (Universidad Finis Terrae, Chile); 2025 44th Int. Conf. of the Chilean Computer Science Society (SCCC), IEEE; doi:10.1109/SCCC67219.2025.11420775
Game / environment: Custom Spelunky-inspired level generator (room templates from Spelunky Classic source code); Super Mario Bros + SMB2 (Lost Levels) level dataset used to calibrate agent restriction weights (pp.2-4)
Role of PCG: Both. Built a Spelunky-style generator as testbed and its main contribution is evaluating its levels.
AI technique: Rule/search-based  (physics-aware A* platformer pathfinding)
Agent / persona: Persona-based (14 agent profiles, each with different mechanic restrictions as a proxy for player abilities/play styles) (pp.1, 3)
Human data?: No - no player data; real SMB levels are used only to calibrate restriction weights (p.4)
Tools / benchmarks: A* Platformer (adapted from Branicki's Unity implementation), Spelunky Classic room templates, SMB level dataset (Summerville & Mateas) (pp.3-4)
Metrics: Proposed: absolute dynamic diversity (DivDA), relative dynamic diversity (DivDR), agent restriction weight (RG), level specific restriction (RL), dynamic difficulty (DifD). Compared with: structural diversity (normalised Levenshtein distance of action sequences) and structural difficulty (path length / nodes explored), both from Beukman et al. Statistics: Mantel test, Spearman correlation (pp.4-6)
Scale: 1,000 generated levels; 14 agent profiles; SMB/SMB2 calibration set (number of levels NR) (pp.1, 4-5)
Key results (+page): At low alpha, relative dynamic diversity correlates strongly with structural diversity (r > 0.5, p < 0.001), and the correlation weakens as the completeness term's weight grows, so mechanic restrictions add information structural metrics miss (p.7, Fig.7). Dynamic difficulty correlates weakly with structural difficulty for all gamma/delta values, and this holds in all 4 structural groups (pp.7-8, Figs.11-12; exact r values only in figures). The authors conclude that difficulty and diversity emerge from the interaction between mechanics and level structure (p.8).
Stated limitations: No limitations section. Implicit: A*-based structural difficulty may not match human-perceived difficulty (p.8); 'diversity' is really an intra-level accessibility measure (p.4); restriction weights assume one active restriction per profile (p.4)
Future work: Reinforcement learning and more sophisticated ways of generating agent populations; richer agent mechanics; evaluating levels in other contexts; industrial use in level design and automated evaluation (p.8)
RQ1 Methods/tools: Spelunky-style template generator + physics-aware A* agent; agent profiles defined as forbidden run-length-encoded action patterns with backtracking; 3-stage traversability pipeline (structural A*, base agent, restricted profiles) (pp.2-4)
RQ2 Properties evaluated: Difficulty, diversity (within a level and between levels), traversability/completability (pp.3-5)
RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: Proposed metrics are compared with established structural metrics (Beukman et al. 2022) using Mantel/Spearman tests. No human validation and no comparison with other generators or SOTA agents (RL, MCTS). Weights are calibrated on real SMB levels (pp.4-7).
RQ4 Limitations/open problems: No evidence that the metrics match human-perceived difficulty; A* agents are not human-like; single genre and single generator; correlation values for difficulty are only shown in figures (pp.7-8)
Reviewer comment: Strong fit for the 'agents with different abilities as playtesters for PCG' theme; compare with persona-based papers P02, P07, P12. Low correlation with existing metrics is presented as 'new insight', but without human ground truth it cannot be told apart from noise; flag this in the synthesis. Includes its own mini-SLR (35 papers) claiming no prior work combines mechanic-constrained agents with level structure (p.2, p.7). Ref [28] looks mislabelled (title says Spelunky, URL is the Mario dataset). Page numbers are PDF pages 1-8 (proceedings page range not printed).
Comparison baseline: Earlier tool (existing structural metrics from Beukman et al. [2])
Testing budget: NR (1,000 levels x 14 profiles; runtime/compute not reported)
Testing objective: Difficulty evaluation, diversity evaluation, traversability/completability

Title (auto): A Rapid and Automated Difficulty Evaluation Framework for Rhythm Games via Persona-Driven Multi-Task Behavioral Cloning
Authors/Year/Venue: Gil, H. and Kang, S. (2026). IEEE Access, vol. 14, pp. 107427-107441. DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2026.3712365
Game / environment: Unnamed proprietary pre-release 8-lane rhythm game built in Unity 6 (main study). osu!mania 4K and 7K and StepMania 4-panel charts for zero-shot external validation
Setting: Both (university authors, proprietary in-development game, framed as internal QA workflow for small and medium studios)
Role of PCG: Generator evaluated (minor, 15 of 45 beatmaps are procedurally generated and are tested by the persona agents alongside human-crafted ones, generation method not described)
AI technique: Behavioural cloning (multi-task Bi-GRU network with hit-probability and timing-offset heads)
Agent / persona: Persona-based (Beginner, Normal, Expert personas, human-like errors rather than optimal play)
Human data?: Yes. Human study for validation (5 annotators Likert rating, 9 raters pairwise comparison) and StepMania human-authored difficulty labels. Origin of the cloned execution labels in the PlayLogs is not clearly explained
Tools / benchmarks: Unity 6 telemetry module, Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.0, NVIDIA RTX 4060 Ti. osu!mania and StepMania charts as external benchmark. Reproducibility package with splits and seeds (data proprietary)
Metrics: Spearman rank correlation vs proxy tiers and external labels, MAE of timing offset, tier MAE, pairwise ranking agreement, ICC and Krippendorff alpha for raters, per-persona miss rate and timing offset, runtime
Scale: 1 proprietary game, 45 beatmaps (15 human-crafted, 15 procedurally generated, 15 naive-random) plus 5-track hidden test set, 3 personas, 287 external charts from 2 commercial games (51 osu!mania 7K, 51 osu!mania 4K, 185 StepMania), 5 plus 9 human raters, 5-fold cross-validation
Key results (+page): Hybrid fusion reaches Spearman 0.949 vs proxy tiers, compared with 0.790 for NPC only, 0.544 for Beginner survival and 0.310 for Normal offset (p.107433). MT-BCN beats 1D-CNN, RNN and LSTM (rho 0.982 +/- 0.004, Cohen d 1.85) but a simple ordinal regression on 11 song features reaches 0.896, showing the proxy labels are largely explained by surface statistics (pp.107435-107436). Zero-shot on 287 osu!mania and StepMania charts gives rho 0.88 to 0.98 with 95 to 100 percent mid-tier pairwise agreement, though NPC alone is similarly strong there (pp.107436-107437). Pairwise human study agrees on 74.1 percent of extreme-tier comparisons (p below 1e-5), Likert study fails (ICC 0.227). Procedural tracks cause about 15 to 20 percent higher Beginner miss rate than human-crafted ones at similar density. 45 beatmaps tiered in about 4.5 s (pp.107437-107438).
Stated limitations: Main rho 0.949 is measured against proxy tiers derived from the pipeline's own persona terms, so it shows coherence not human agreement. Human validation covers only extreme tiers (Likert N 5 unreliable, pairwise N 9). Static chart stimuli miss timing, audio and motor load. Small proprietary corpus of 45 beatmaps for one 8-lane layout, weights need recalibration elsewhere. Single pre-release game without player telemetry. Normal and Expert offset terms did not transfer externally and easiest charts are poorly separated. No deployment or cost study (p.107440).
Future work: Validate against post-launch player telemetry, run a larger human study with audiovisual playthrough stimuli and rhythm-game specialist annotators, add explainable-AI tooling on top of the per-persona outputs for designers (pp.107439-107440).
RQ1 Methods/tools: Persona-driven multi-task behavioural cloning (Bi-GRU) with invincibility-mode simulation so agents play full beatmaps, persona terms fused with NPC into a hybrid score and quantized into 15 difficulty tiers. Implemented in Unity 6 and PyTorch (pp.107429-107432).
RQ2 Properties evaluated: Difficulty, split into cognitive overload (Beginner miss rate), execution error (Normal offset) and biomechanical ceiling (Expert offset). Also detects unplayable clutter and awkward unintuitive transitions in procedurally generated tracks (p.107437).
RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: Established practice is the NPC density heuristic used in industry. Learned baselines are 1D-CNN, RNN, LSTM, Random Forest, Bi-LSTM, Transformer and ordinal regression. Validation combines proxy tiers, zero-shot external datasets with independent labels and a two-stage human study. Authors explicitly treat in-sample rho as circular and argue DRL agents are unsuitable because they converge to superhuman play (p.107435).
RQ4 Limitations/open problems: Lack of independent ground truth for difficulty (proxy label circularity), unreliable chart-based human ratings, mid-tier difficulty not validated by humans, biomechanical terms not transferable across games, no player telemetry before release, generated content only lightly examined.
Reviewer comment: Strong, self-critical evaluation (circularity diagnostic, external datasets, honest limitations). Limited PCG evidence since only 15 generated beatmaps are tested and one short paragraph reports what the agents found on them (higher miss rate, awkward transitions), so mainly useful for RQ2 and RQ3 as a difficulty-testing method. Persona idea cites procedural personas (Holmgard et al., P12). Note NPC means Note Placement Complexity. 15 tiers not 16.
Comparison baseline: Earlier tool (NPC heuristic), Model-based (1D-CNN, RNN, LSTM, Random Forest, Bi-LSTM, Transformer, ordinal regression), Human (pairwise study)
Testing budget: About 4.5 s end-to-end for 45 beatmaps on RTX 4060 Ti, training up to 100 epochs with early stopping (patience 15), extended baselines at 20 epochs
Testing objective: Difficulty estimation and tiering of beatmaps, including flagging unplayable or awkward patterns

Title (auto): Artificial Players in the Design Process: Developing an Automated Testing Tool for Game Level and World Design
Authors/Year/Venue: Stahlke, S., Nova, A. & Mirza-Babaei, P. (Ontario Tech University, Canada); CHI PLAY '20 (Annual Symposium on Computer-Human Interaction in Play), Virtual Event, 2-4 Nov 2020, ACM, pp.267-280; doi:10.1145/3410404.3414249
Game / environment: PathOS, an open-source Unity extension for any 3D first/third-person game with ground-plane navigation. In the user study, participants built 2 levels for a hypothetical action-adventure game from provided Unity prefabs (pp.270, 273, 276)
Genre: Other (3D action-adventure / open-world level and world design)
Setting: Academic (study participants are game developers and industry professionals)
Role of PCG: Not PCG (testing only). PCG appears only as a use case one participant suggested (pp.275, 277)
AI technique: Rule-search (hand-crafted cognitive architecture: perception, memory and motive-weighted destination scoring over Unity navmesh pathfinding; no learning) (pp.270-272)
Agent / persona: Persona-based (motivation profiles of 7 weighted motives from player typologies: curiosity, achievement, completion, aggression, adrenaline, caution, efficiency; plus an 'experience' parameter; human-like perception and memory limits) (pp.270-271)
Human data?: Yes. A qualitative user study with 9 game developers (interviews plus a take-home level design exercise) evaluates the tool. No human player data is used to build or validate the agents (pp.273, 278)
Tools / benchmarks: PathOS (open source: github.com/samanthastahlke/pathos), Unity engine (navmesh, physics, raycasting), C# (p.270)
Metrics: Tool outputs: agent path traces, heatmap of time spent per area, proportion of agents visiting each tagged entity (p.272). Study measures: deductive qualitative coding of post-exercise interviews (positive/negative/change per category and per feature); counts of participants who used the tool and changed their levels (pp.273-274)
Validation approach: Human study (qualitative developer study; agent behaviour not compared with human players)
Scale: 10 participants recruited, 9 completed (1 withdrew), 8 did the full take-home exercise (one built only 1 level); exercise about 2-3 h; interviews 30-45 min before and 40-60 min after; 2 coders (pp.273-274)
Key results (+page): All 8 participants who did the exercise used PathOS to test their levels; 4 never (P6, P7) or rarely (P1, P9) playtested themselves and relied on the agents (p.274). 5 of 8 changed their levels after watching the agents, e.g. blocking unintended shortcuts, opening more paths, adding objects (p.274). All 9 called the tool useful, citing time/labour savings and easier recruitment (p.275). 7 of 9 thought it could also serve QA (p.277). Opinions on whether agent behaviour was believable were mixed (p.275). The authors conclude it gives actionable feedback at much lower cost than human usertesting (p.277).

Title (auto): Automated Gameplay Testing and Validation With Curiosity-Conditioned Proximal Trajectories

AI technique: Hybrid (deep RL with PPO + adversarial imitation learning with AMP/GAIL + curiosity via random network distillation)
Agent / persona: Curiosity-driven (exploration-conditioned: alpha, sampled per episode and given as input, moves the agent from imitating expert demonstrations (alpha=0) to pure exploration (alpha=1)) (p.117)

Scale: 1 custom environment with 4 goal areas; 6 expert demonstrations per area; 10 agents in parallel; 30,000 episodes x 500 timesteps per experiment; ablation 50,000 episodes, 5 runs; 1 ViZDoom level; 5 professional level designers (pp.121-124)

RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: Compared with SOTA RL baselines: Gordillo et al. 2021 curiosity-only agents, AMP imitation-only, and a linear curiosity+imitation mix; ablations against normalised or learned position encodings and raycasting. Title (auto): Automated Play-Testing Through RL Based Human-Like Play-Styles Generation

Game / environment: In-house turn-based strategic shooter built with Unity ML-Agents, inspired by Mario + Rabbids (3 heroes vs up to 7 behaviour-tree enemies, 20x20 grid, 10 turns max)
Setting: Both (Sorbonne Universite LIP6 and Ubisoft La Forge)
AI technique: RL (goal-conditioned RL with ACER, ALP-GMM curriculum, GMM clustering of player data)
Agent / persona: Human-like (single agent conditioned on target play-style relative to player population, GMM clusters of players act as personas)
Human data?: Yes. Summary data (5 per-turn metrics plus outcomes) from a play session, 30 recruited, 25 used, about 1 h each on 10 levels. No full trajectories
Tools / benchmarks: Unity ML-Agents, ACER, prioritized replay, ALP-GMM automatic curriculum, Gaussian mixture model clustering, 12-core CPU with GTX 1070
Metrics: KL and JS divergence between agent and player metric distributions, per-turn shots, stabs, empower, heal and shield per cluster (mean, 95 percent CI), win, loss and draw rates, play-style coverage plots
Scale: 1 game, 10 hand-designed levels (level 1 dropped, 7 train, 2 test), 25 players (175 training data points), 3 agents (CARMI, CARI, WinOnly), 3 player clusters, 5 metrics, 2500 coverage episodes
Key results (+page): CARMI covers the players' play-style space and also reaches styles players never used, unlike CARI (p.150). On train levels CARMI is closest to players (KL 6.69 vs 9.34 CARI and 10.17 WinOnly, JS 0.60 vs 0.73 and 0.76), but on test levels the three are similar (KL 9.74 vs 9.38 vs 9.53, JS 0.78 vs 0.80 vs 0.80) (p.151). On unseen levels CARMI predicts the right trend, players win more overall (88 to 95 percent) and so does CARMI (68 to 74 percent), and it mirrors the drop for cluster 3 (players 87 to 75, CARMI 67 to 52) (pp.151-152). WinOnly wins only 33 percent and misses super-ability use entirely, so it gives misleading difficulty feedback (p.152).
Stated limitations: Only 5 play-modes capture play-style. Training levels are limited to those with human data (7). Agent vs player gaps are larger per cluster than for the whole population. Whole-episode metrics can be met in unexpected ways in long games such as RTS, giving misleading feedback. Generates human-like play-styles, not human-like behaviour, since no full trajectories are used (pp.148, 152).
Future work: Add more play-modes and study the effect of the number of metrics, train on randomly generated levels or variations without human data to improve generalisation, use the player cluster distribution during training (p.152).
RQ1 Methods/tools: CARMI, a configurable goal-conditioned RL agent whose input is a target play-style expressed as metrics normalised against the player distribution per level, trained once with ACER and an ALP-GMM curriculum. GMM clusters of player data are sampled to emulate human play-styles on new levels (pp.148-150).
RQ2 Properties evaluated: Difficulty per play-style (win, loss, draw rates) and play-style fidelity (shots, stabs, empower, heal, shield per turn) on hand-designed levels, plus coverage of the human play-style space. No generated content tested.
RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: Compared against the authors' earlier CARI agent (CoG 2021) and a WinOnly RL agent representing common industry practice, all judged against real player summary data on held-out levels with KL and JS divergence and cluster metrics. Argues win-only RL is the established but misleading practice. No statistical tests and only 2 test levels.
RQ4 Limitations/open problems: Human data scarcity limits training levels, few metrics define play-style, poorer per-cluster fit, risk of metric gaming in long-episode games, and agents still win far less often than players (68 vs 88 percent).
Reviewer comment: Included under the eligibility rule (automated method plus evaluation), no PCG match in the tested content since all levels are hand-made, though the method targets unseen new levels and the authors propose generated levels for training. Test-level KL and JS show no clear advantage over baselines although the authors claim reliable generalisation, and the agent underestimates absolute win rates, so only relative difficulty trends are supported. Cites Holmgard et al. 2019 (P12) and Sestini et al. CCPT (P10). Genre is turn-based strategy, not RTS.
Comparison baseline: Earlier tool (CARI, CoG 2021), Other (WinOnly RL agent), Human (player summary data)
Testing budget: About 24 h training on one machine (12-core CPU, GTX 1070), 3 parallel environments of about 12,500 episodes each, 2500 episodes for coverage analysis (p.150)
Testing objective: Difficulty and balancing feedback per human-like play-style on new levels

Title (auto): Coverage-Aware Guidance for Novelty-Driven Exploration in Automated Game Testing Under Sparse-Reward 3-D Environments
Authors/Year/Venue: Jang, T.-H., Lee, H.-U. and Kim, H. (2026). IEEE Access, vol. 14, pp. 137393-137407. DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2026.3730445
Game / environment: Minecraft via Project Malmo, two custom maps (randomized 21x21 DFS-generated maze for exploration, fixed hand-made 20x20 four-room arena with 10 seeded faults for bug finding)
Role of PCG: Generator evaluated (partial, agents explore 50 DFS-generated maze instances for coverage only, all bug testing happens in a hand-made arena)
AI technique: RL (DQN with RND novelty reward plus CAE count-based coverage reward and stagnation recovery bonus)
Agent / persona: Curiosity-driven (novelty and coverage intrinsic rewards)
Human data?: No
Tools / benchmarks: Minecraft, Project Malmo Python API with XML missions, DQN, RND, RELINE and BEAGT as baselines, Issue-10 seeded-fault benchmark built by the authors
Metrics: Cumulative best-so-far coverage AUC, final coverage, final unique bug count, bug discovery AUC, per-fault discovery rate, steps to first, third and fifth bug, bootstrap 95 percent CI, permutation tests, Cliff's delta
Scale: 2 environments, 50 generated mazes, 1 arena with 10 seeded faults, 6 methods plus 2 ablation variants, 10 seeded runs per method in the arena
Key results (+page): In the maze RND+CAE has the highest coverage AUC (22.09 +/- 2.80 vs 21.48 +/- 4.38 for RND) but final coverage is the same (27.64 vs 27.69 percent), and CAE alone is not better than RND (pp.137402-137403). In the arena RND+CAE finds the most bugs (5.70 +/- 1.06 of 10, AUC 4.66) and clearly beats Random (3.50, +2.20 bugs, p below 0.001, Cliff's delta 0.95), but differences vs RELINE, RND, CAE and BEAGT are not significant (CIs cross zero) (p.137403). Gains come from a few faults (slot desync 50 vs 20 percent, break event 40 vs 10 percent) and one fault was never found by any method (p.137404). Ablation shows spatial-only coverage matches Full (5.80 vs 5.70 bugs), while removing stagnation recovery drops AUC to 4.09 (p 0.035) and runs reaching five bugs from 90 to 70 percent (p.137404).
Stated limitations: RND is already a strong baseline and CAE alone does not beat it. Only 10 runs per method and most differences from learned baselines are not significant. Gains are concentrated in a few fault types. CAE coverage is an implementation-dependent abstraction because semantic metadata was not available. Individual coverage keys were not ablated and stagnation-trigger logs were missing for Full. Only one maze family and one fixed arena with predefined faults, so no evidence for unseen layouts, larger worlds or other engines. Seeded faults abstract real bug patterns rather than reproduce real bugs (pp.137400, 137405).
Future work: Individual-key ablations, unseen layouts and triggers, larger environments, action-sequence novelty, targeted local fuzzing, hierarchical policies combining navigation with local interaction testing, and later validation of disaster-response simulations (p.137406).
RQ1 Methods/tools: RND+CAE, a DQN agent whose intrinsic reward combines RND prediction-error novelty with CAE visitation counts over environment-adapted coverage keys (cell, state-action, action sequence) and a one-step stagnation recovery bonus, run in Minecraft through Project Malmo (pp.137396-137398).
RQ2 Properties evaluated: Spatial coverage of procedurally generated mazes and discovery of interaction-dependent seeded functional faults (state transition, movement, physics, inventory and input desync) in a fixed arena. Generated mazes are explored but not tested for defects.
RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: Compared with Random, RELINE (established RL testing baseline), BEAGT (reward-trend adaptive exploration), RND and CAE alone under the same 100k-step budget, with bootstrap CIs, permutation tests and effect sizes. Clear gain over Random, only numerical gains over learned baselines, so RND and RELINE remain strong reference points.
RQ4 Limitations/open problems: Sparse rewards and exploration stagnation in 3D games, reaching a fault region does not guarantee triggering it, seeded faults instead of real bugs, no generalisation to unseen layouts or other engines, small number of runs limits statistical power.
Reviewer comment: Careful and honest statistics, the authors themselves say most gains over learned baselines are not established. PCG partly relevant since generated mazes are only used to measure exploration. RELINE (ref 17, Tufano et al. ICSE 2022) is P24, cross-check during synthesis. No code link given.
Comparison baseline: Random, Earlier tool (RELINE, BEAGT, RND)
Testing budget: 100,000 training steps per run, 90 s arena episodes, logging every 1000 steps, 10 seeded runs per method in the arena, hardware NR
Testing objective: Failure detection (seeded interaction-dependent functional bugs) and spatial exploration coverage

Title (auto): Advancing Level Generation in Super Mario Bros.: A Proposal for Combining Diffusion Models with Real-Time Playability Assessment

Game / environment: Super Mario Bros via the Mario AI framework, MarioPuzzle (the authors' endless level generation framework in OpenAI Gym)
Primary goal: Level validation (included narrowly, the paper's main aim is generating fun, diverse and playable endless levels, the testing role is automated playability checking of generated segments)

Agent / persona: Goal-driven (A* agent plays to reach the end of each segment)

Tools / benchmarks: Mario AI framework A* agent, MarioGAN, CNet-assisted evolutionary repairer, OpenAI Gym, PPO, VGLC levels. Code released on GitHub (mariopuzzle)
Metrics: Playability P (number of segments out of 100 the A* agent completes), fun F and Fb (percent of segments within moderate diversity bounds), historical deviation H, counts of gaps, pipes, enemies, coins and blocks, failed generations, unplayable segments, resamples, faulty tiles before and after repair, generation time per segment
Scale: 1 game, 7 reward variants plus 1 random designer, 300 levels per agent (30 start segments x 10 runs, up to 100 segments each), 300 online levels of 100 playable segments for the best agent, 3 human players for timing
Key results (+page): Designers trained with the playability reward produce far more playable levels, average P 97.4 of 100 segments for the full fun plus deviation plus playability agent vs 16.0 for the random designer and 16.4 without playability (p.6, Table II). Because the A* tester is predictable, the designer learns to add ground tiles and produce linear levels with few gaps and little exploration (pp.7-8).
Stated limitations: Generated levels depend strongly on the behaviour of the A* test agent, which yields linear, easy levels with limited gaps and exploration. Fun and deviation are theory-driven proxies not tested with human players. The repairer satisfies logic constraints but does not guarantee playability. Only one game (SMB) and only level content tested. Reward terms combined with fixed weights (pp.7-8).
Future work: Use various human-like test agents and continuously train the designer from their play, cross-verify reward functions against human players, add surprise, novelty and flow-based difficulty metrics, multi-objective optimisation of quality and diversity, intrinsic motivation and curiosity views, scale to more complex games and other content types (p.8).
RQ1 Methods/tools: Testing component is an off-the-shelf A* agent from the Mario AI framework used as an automated playtester inside the generation loop, its pass or fail result both ends RL training episodes and triggers resampling of unplayable segments online (pp.4-5, 7). Pattern of tester-in-the-loop generation.
RQ2 Properties evaluated: Playability or completability of each generated segment by the A* agent, plus content metrics (fun as moderate diversity, historical deviation, faulty tiles, level element counts).
RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: The generator is compared with a random latent-space designer and reward ablations with and without playability. The tester itself is not evaluated or compared with other testers. A* playability checking is used as established practice in Mario PCG research.

Title (auto): It might be balanced, but is it actually good? An Empirical Evaluation of Game Level Balancing

Authors/Year/Venue: Mu, E., Yoda, M., Zhang, Y., Zhang, M., Matsuno, Y. and Li, J. (2026). Entertainment Computing, vol. 58, article 101185 (Elsevier)
Game / environment: Overcooked (open-source research toolkit), Minecraft (scripted environment with high-level commands), MineDojo (Minecraft research framework with programmatically generated tasks)
Primary goal: Coverage-exploration (coverage of modified code after a game update while completing the new gameplay tasks)
Role of PCG: Not PCG (testing only), MineDojo's procedurally generated worlds and tasks are used as one test environment for its diversity
AI technique: Hybrid (LLM, GPT-5, reads the AST code diff and produces ordered subgoals, reward functions and code anchors, then a PPO RL agent is trained on a hybrid semantic plus structural coverage reward)
Agent / persona: Goal-driven (follows LLM-generated subgoal sequence, with an extra reward for covering changed code)
Human data?: No
Tools / benchmarks: GPT-5 via OpenAI API (DeepSeek-V3 in sensitivity test), AST differencing, pytest-based code instrumentation, Stable-Baselines3 PPO, Overcooked toolkit, Minecraft, MineDojo, RTX 4070 Ti
Metrics: Line coverage and branch coverage of modified code, anchor discovery, task success rate, unique states, Ngram-3 action diversity, mean episode length, anchor mapping precision, recall and F1
Scale: 3 environments, 46 update tasks (21 Overcooked, 20 Minecraft, 5 MineDojo), about 180 to 320 changed lines and 100 to 150 changed branches per environment, 7 methods including 4 SMART variants, 5 seeds each
Key results (+page): SMART-Full reaches line and branch coverage of 0.93 and 0.98 in Overcooked, 0.92 and 0.94 in Minecraft and 0.76 and 0.72 in MineDojo, vs 0.55 and 0.58, 0.46 and 0.51, 0.34 and 0.31 for plain PPO, while keeping task success at 0.98, 0.98 and 0.79 vs 0.65, 0.70 and 0.51 (p.8, Tables 1 to 3). The curiosity baseline PPO+ICM visits the most unique states but finds far fewer changed-code anchors (166.86 vs 289.71 in Overcooked), so state novelty is not code novelty (p.8). Ablations show semantic-only reward completes tasks (about 97 percent) but covers only about half the changed code, and structural-only or global rewards collapse to near 0 success (p.8). Only code logic changes are handled, not UI, 3D assets, shaders or neural AI behaviour. Messy, poorly structured codebases weaken diffing and intent extraction. Agents can game the structural reward by triggering the same code region repeatedly (pp.10-11).
Future work: Closed-loop refinement and human-in-the-loop checks of low-confidence LLM subgoals, multi-modal analysis for non-code updates (assets, UI, data tables), combining with symbolic execution or fuzzing for hard-to-reach branches, hierarchical or DAG-based subgoals for long and non-linear gameplay, testing other update types such as removals and refactorings (pp.11, 13).

RQ2 Properties evaluated: Structural coverage of updated code (lines, branches, anchors) and functional completion of the new gameplay tasks. No real or seeded bugs are counted, defect detection is only illustrated with one hypothetical case (oven timeout branch, p.10).
RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: Compared with Random, PPO (task-only RL) and PPO+ICM (curiosity), described by the authors as state of the art general game testing agents, plus three ablations, all with the same PPO setup and budget over 5 seeds. Code-coverage regression tools such as GameRTS are discussed but not compared. Shows a gap between curiosity-driven exploration and targeted code coverage.
RQ4 Limitations/open problems: Coverage is used as a proxy for bug detection, dependence on LLM correctness, reward gaming, no handling of non-code or dynamic changes, only element-addition updates tested on research environments rather than commercial codebases.
Reviewer comment: Strong, well-controlled update-testing study, but it measures code coverage and task success, not bugs found. Baselines are generic RL agents rather than earlier testing tools. GameRTS (ref 18) is P28 and Wuji and Ariyurek et al. are cited, useful for RQ3 cross-checks. Weak PCG link, only MineDojo's generated tasks. Data available on request only.
Comparison baseline: Random, Model-based (PPO task-only RL and PPO+ICM curiosity agent), plus ablations (Semantic-only, Structural-only, Global-Hybrid)
Testing budget: Per task 100K steps (Overcooked), 1M (Minecraft), 1.5M (MineDojo), 5 seeds, about 15 to 20 min, 2 to 3 h and 3 to 4 h per task on one RTX 4070 Ti, plus 138 GPT-5 calls in under 30 min in total (p.7)

AI technique: Evolutionary (neuroevolution with NEAT evolving network weights and topology, fitness from approach level, branch distance and control flow distance)

Human data?: No

Metrics: Reliable block coverage across random seeds, number of winning states reached, coverage drop between generation and re-execution, mutation score, false-positive rate, Mann-Whitney U test and Vargha-Delaney A12
Scale: 25 games, 30 repetitions for RQ1, 10 dynamic and 10 static suites per game each run on 10 new seeds for RQ2, 8 mutation operators with up to 50 mutants per operator for RQ3, population 300 networks
Key results (+page): Neatest reaches 94.60 percent mean reliable coverage vs 89.07 percent for random testing and wins games about 20 of 30 times vs 5 (p.9, Table 3). It covers more in 22 games, ties in 2 and loses in 1 (CityDefender), and reaches a winning state in 22 of 25 games (p.9). Stated limitations: Only 25 Scratch games, so results may not generalise to other Scratch programs or other languages. Randomness in experiments and an experimentally chosen surprise threshold that may not suit other programs. Search budget of 23 h is long. Future work: Combine Neatest with backpropagation to cut search time, use newer neuroevolution variants, adapt to Android and iOS games (needs feature extraction and play loop engineering), apply to randomised non-game programs such as flaky tests, explore alternative surprise adequacy metrics (pp.10-11).
RQ1 Methods/tools: Neatest, a NEAT-based test generator that evolves neural networks to play Scratch games so that they reliably reach target statements despite randomness, then reuses the trained networks as test oracles by comparing activations on a changed program using surprise adequacy (pp.3-7).

RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: Compared with a random test generator (RQ1) and static input-sequence tests extracted from the same runs (RQ2), with 30 repetitions and nonparametric statistics, and mutation analysis for the oracle (RQ3). Shows adaptive learned agents beat static and random tests on randomised games. No comparison with other learning-based game testers.
RQ4 Limitations/open problems: High search cost, small educational games only, oracle false positives, mutants as a proxy for real faults, and difficulty with games needing complex strategies.
Reviewer comment: Strong SE-venue paper with open artifact and clear statistics. One of few papers measuring fault detection (mutation score) rather than only coverage. Subjects are small Scratch games, so external validity for commercial or PCG games is limited. PCG not involved, randomised runtime behaviour is not generated content. Same group as Deiner et al. (Scratch test generation), a candidate found earlier.

Testing budget: 23 h search per game with 10x acceleration, playthroughs up to 10 s (100 s game time), population 300, 30 repetitions (p.8)
Testing objective: Failure detection and reliable statement coverage, including reaching winning states, for games with randomised behaviour

Key results (+page): The object-level approach detects all 24 injected bugs (100 percent accuracy) with MSE, SSIM or embedding similarity, vs 44.6 percent for traditional snapshot testing (pp.1, 8, Table 3 p.10). RQ2 Properties evaluated: Performance (frame-rate drops / rendering time) in areas real players would reach; agents must still play competently to reach them (pp.2, 5-6)
RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: Compared with an RL agent trained only to play and a random agent, using 10 trainings (proof of concept), significance tests with Holm correction and effect sizes. Ground truth only exists for the injected bugs; no developer confirmation that the SuperTuxKart points are real issues. Stated limitations: Balance depends on heuristic scripted players, simulation cost is high, rewards are sparse, only a simplified 6x6 game with four tile types and no combat
Future work: Human playtests to validate balance, balancing for different player types, cheaper surrogate reward models, other domains such as urban planning
RQ1 Methods/tools: Three-part architecture of level generator, balancing agent and simulation, with simulation-driven rewards and new swap-based PCGRL representations. Testing is done by scripted agents, RL does the editing
RQ2 Properties evaluated: Competitive balance (win rate parity), playability, distance from the target balance, number of edits and diversity of generated levels
RQ3 Evaluation & baselines (established: Original PCGRL narrow representation and two hill-climbing search baselines on 1000 levels, reported as shares of balanced and improved levels. No human validation of balance
RQ4 Limitations/open problems: Balance is only as good as the scripted agents, simulation cost, sparse rewards, small simplified game, no human check
Reviewer comment: Strongest explicit PCG paper in the set and code is public (Q2 = 1). It is mainly a PCG and balancing method, so it fits the generation-papers rule only narrowly, like P15. The automated tester is a scripted agent and not an AI method, and balance is validated only by those same agents (circular, like P07). Venue and DOI taken from the arXiv record, the preprint PDF has no volume or pages
Comparison baseline: Search (hill climbing) and Earlier tool (original PCGRL)
Testing budget: 14 simulated matches per balancing action, 200 000 training steps in the main comparison, hill climbing capped at 8 changes
Testing objective: Reach a target win rate balance (mostly 50 and 50) with few tile changes while keeping levels playable
